description:
We are a passionate team interested in space, health, genetics, and innovative technology.

We bring skills in AI/ML, software development, data science, and creative problem-solving.
summary: AstroCare is an offline, evidence-first health console for astronauts, from launch to recovery. It helps crew members and flight surgeons see what changed in a person's health, when, how the system knows, and what to do next, even when a doctor on Earth is minutes away. It uses machine learning only where NASA data support it (a solar particle storm forecaster trained on DONKI/GOES history and a blood gene-expression radiation biodosimeter trained on OSDR studies), and compares everything else, such as vitals, immune panels, microbiome, and recovery, with each person's own pre-flight baseline using transparent rules. Every value shows its source, its rule, and a safe, non-diagnostic next step.
details:
THE CHALLENGE

Astronauts face health risks they cannot feel, such as radiation, microgravity and isolation. Their health data sit in separate systems, and on the way to Mars a message to a doctor can take up to 20 minutes each way. Crews will therefore need to check their own health and act sensibly before help can answer.

Most health software either predicts without enough data or hides the evidence behind a single score. AstroCare does the opposite.


HOW IT WORKS

AstroCare brings nine health domains into one console and treats each one according to the strength of the evidence behind it. We call this our "evidence gate."

Where the data are strong enough, AstroCare uses machine learning. The M1 Solar Storm Early Warning module is a calibrated logistic regression trained on NASA DONKI flare records and NOAA GOES proton data from 2010 to 2023. On the untouched 2024–2026 test period, it warned of 14 of 21 storms, including the May 2024 storm, with a ROC-AUC of 0.81. The M3 Blood Biodosimeter uses elastic-net models trained on NASA OSDR human blood studies (OSD-1012 and OSD-410). It was validated leave-one-donor-out, with a mean absolute error of 0.38 Gy at 24 hours, and externally tested on OSD-71. M3 refuses to answer outside its validated time windows or when the person's own baseline sample is missing.

Where physics gives a better answer than data, AstroCare uses physics. The M2 Crew Dose module combines the MSL/RAD cosmic-ray rate with storm proton flux and shielding level (habitat, shelter or EVA), and shows the result against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

Where only a few people have been measured, AstroCare compares each person with their own baseline instead of training a model. The M4 Microbiome, M7 Immune and M6 Recovery modules apply rules against each Inspiration4 crew member's own pre-flight samples (OSD-572, OSD-575 and OSD-569), with thresholds calibrated on pre-flight data only. Of the changes seen the day after landing, 74% were back within the crew member's own normal variation by R+82. Similarly, M9 Daily Vitals uses a robust modified z-score to compare heart rate, HRV, SpO2 and respiratory rate against the astronaut's own previous 30 days, alongside cabin CO2. Four crew members are too few to train a model honestly, so these domains use rules, not ML.

Where per-person data are too thin to produce numbers, AstroCare shows published evidence instead. M5 Brain and M8 Telomere appear as evidence cards. A Body & Mind section adds a daily self-check, a reaction-time test and bone scan tracking.

Every flag opens an explanation card that shows what changed, when it changed, which rule fired and which study supports it. A rule-based Action Center then suggests a safe next step, such as "repeat the measurement" or "review with the flight surgeon." AstroCare never names a disease or a medication, and never reduces health to a single score. Every value carries one of seven provenance labels (measured, derived, ML-predicted, estimated, context, self-reported or telemetry), so a prediction is never confused with a measurement.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

AstroCare runs on a Python backend with 33 API endpoints, served either through FastAPI or a zero-install built-in server. The front end is a 12-page web console built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Three.js, supported by versioned rules and a 14-entry evidence registry. The whole system runs fully offline with a single command (python run.py). There are 26 automated tests. They check that the software reproduces the notebook results exactly, refuses invalid inputs, contains no diagnostic wording and gives every value a provenance label.

WHO IT HELPS

AstroCare is built for three groups. Astronauts on board use it to monitor their own health. Flight surgeons use it to review flags together with the evidence behind them. Researchers get provenance-labelled data, methods and code.

LIMITATIONS

The Inspiration4 data cover only four crew members, so those results are descriptive rather than generalizable. M1 produces many false alerts, and M3 was trained on Earth blood irradiated outside the body. The mission vitals are a reconstructed scenario, not data from a flown crew.

WHAT WE'D BUILD NEXT

OSD-1012: Human blood, X-ray and neutron (24 h)Our next step is to calibrate M2 against MSL/RAD measurements from real solar storms. We also plan to connect real wearable streams to M9 and add the OSD-656 urine panel to M7. For M3, we want to validate the models on more independent datasets and, when it becomes available, on in-flight blood. Finally, we aim to test the console with flight surgeons and add live DONKI and GOES feeds whenever a link to Earth exists.
